source_title: FCC chair wants to let prisons jam illegal cellphones
en_body:
## FCC to Vote on Rule That Would Let Prisons Use Cellphone Jammers

The Federal Communications Commission announced that it will put a proposed rule before its commissioners. The proposal would allow state prisons and jails to opt in to use cellphone jammers. The stated purpose is to stop inmates from using illegal cellphones, which officials say could help inmates continue criminal activity.

The agency said it will hold an open meeting and vote next month, on November 19, on relaxing a long-standing opposition to jammers. The change would not require prisons or jails to use the technology. The FCC has also said that equipment which interferes with communications signals is illegal for non-federal parties to use.

In 2018, the Federal Bureau of Prisons began testing micro-jamming in federal prisons as a way to block unauthorized cellphone use by inmates. The proposed FCC action could open similar tools at state and local levels and provide a formal pathway for federal facilities to jam signals as well.

## Background and Concerns

The FCC has previously not allowed jammers as a method of reducing illegal cellphone use in prisons. Its concerns included possible interference with emergency and public safety communications, as well as creating security risks by putting more jamming tools into the environment where they could be exploited.

If the new rule were adopted, correctional facilities would need to meet standards, including proving that the jamming solution does not cause harmful interference outside designated geographic areas.

## What Is Confirmed and What Is Not

The confirmed facts are narrow. The FCC announced a proposal and a planned vote. The source does not yet establish whether the vote will pass, what final conditions might apply, or how the rule would be implemented. It is also not clear how the proposal would affect federal prisons, state prisons, local jails, emergency communications, or enforcement.

## Practical Implications and Uncertainties

For prison officials, the proposal could offer a technical option for limiting unauthorized cell signal. For the public, the central issue is whether jammers can operate without disrupting emergency communications or creating new security problems. The source does not provide a final assessment of those risks.

## How Readers Can Check

The reported details come from the source article at https://www.engadget.com/2300569/fcc-chair-wants-to-let-prisons-jam-illegal-cellphones/. The FCC has not yet voted, and the source does not include a final rule text, implementation timeline, or independent safety review.
